sourceCheck: Checked 2026-10-03. https://web.dev/articles/vitals, last updated October 31, 2024, identifies LCP, INP and CLS as the current Core Web Vitals, all Stable. Their good thresholds are LCP <= 2.5 s, INP <= 200 ms and CLS <= 0.1; poor values are LCP > 4 s, INP > 500 ms and CLS > 0.25. Assessment uses the 75th percentile of page loads, separately for mobile and desktop. web.dev's general pass rule requires all three to meet their good targets. Threshold reference: https://web.dev/articles/defining-core-web-vitals-thresholds. Supporting metrics remain outside the Core Web Vitals: FCP good <= 1.8 s and poor > 3 s (https://web.dev/articles/fcp); TTFB good <= 800 ms and poor > 1800 ms, with its good target explicitly nonmandatory (https://web.dev/articles/ttfb). CrUX categorizes TTFB as experimental (https://developer.chrome.com/docs/crux/methodology/metrics). The newest monthly CrUX dataset listed is August 2026, published September 8, 2026. The 2026 release notes announce no change to the Core Web Vitals metric set or definitions; the reported INP regression is not an announced metric-definition change. INP replaced FID on March 12, 2024; Search Console removed FID then, while PageSpeed Insights and CrUX had a six-month transition. September 2024 release notes remove FID from the CrUX API and identify August 2024 as the final BigQuery dataset containing FID. References: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/crux/release-notes and https://web.dev/blog/inp-cwv-march-12. Lighthouse 13 is the latest major version verified in the official release documentation: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/lighthouse-13-0. MDN currently labels LargestContentfulPaint and PerformanceEventTiming Baseline 2025, Newly available since December 2025: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/LargestContentfulPaint and https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/PerformanceEventTiming. LayoutShift is Limited availability, not Baseline, and experimental: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/LayoutShift. CLS API measurement remains Chromium-specific, also noted in https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/soft-navigations. Chrome still permits eligible Cache-Control: no-store pages in the bfcache under its documented restrictions; cookie or other authorization changes can evict them. The Chrome-specific reference records the March-April 2025 rollout: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/bfcache-ccns. This supersedes the work-in-progress wording still present in https://web.dev/articles/bfcache. Chrome's unload deprecation disables handlers by default unless a page opts back in. The published schedule reaches full page-load rollout with Chrome 154 on September 22, 2026, but explicitly remains subject to change; this is the documented schedule, not independent confirmation of deployment: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/deprecating-unload. Soft-navigation measurement is enabled by default from Chrome 151, while the exact way CrUX will report soft navigations remains undecided: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/soft-navigations. PageSpeed Insights retains its documented insufficient-INP exception: good LCP and CLS suffice for a pass when INP data is insufficient, distinct from web.dev's general three-metric rule: https://developers.google.com/speed/docs/insights/v5/about. The requested scope remains usable with those qualifications. Reference pages take precedence over stale guide wording: Content-Encoding includes zstd (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Encoding), despite the compression guide's gzip/br emphasis; omitted sizes defaults to 100vw (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/img). The LCP image-size card tests the intrinsic-area cap using the specification's upscaling adjustment, rather than assuming displayed CSS area is the reported area: https://www.w3.org/TR/largest-contentful-paint/.

cards.statement: An LCP of 2.5 seconds falls within the good range.
cards.explanation: The good LCP boundary includes 2.5 seconds. Values above 4 seconds fall in the poor range.

source.title: Defining the Core Web Vitals metrics thresholds

cards.statement: Core Web Vitals assessment uses the median page-load experience.
cards.explanation: Core Web Vitals assessment uses the 75th percentile, which exposes slower experiences that a median can hide.
cards.misconception: The middle observation determines the assessment.

source.title: Defining the Core Web Vitals metrics thresholds

cards.statement: Core Web Vitals assessment pools mobile and desktop visits.
cards.explanation: Core Web Vitals assessment evaluates mobile and desktop page loads separately.
cards.misconception: A combined device sample determines the assessment.

source.title: Defining the Core Web Vitals metrics thresholds

cards.statement: web.dev accepts two good Core Web Vitals out of three as a pass.
cards.explanation: web.dev says tools should award a pass when all three Core Web Vitals meet their good targets.
cards.misconception: The general pass rule permits one metric to miss its target.

cards.statement: INP assesses responsiveness throughout a page visit.
cards.explanation: INP observes responsiveness over the visit, so interactions well after loading remain relevant.

cards.statement: CLS measures the time a layout change takes to render.
cards.explanation: CLS quantifies unexpected visual movement with a unitless score, rather than timing how long rendering takes.
cards.misconception: CLS is a rendering-duration metric.

cards.statement: Pending Web Vitals have a scheduled transition toward Stable status.
cards.explanation: Pending metrics have passed initial testing and feedback, with a timeline set for promotion to Stable.

cards.statement: Stable Web Vitals remain open to definition improvements.
cards.explanation: Stable means established guidance and support, not a frozen definition; corrections and improvements remain possible.

cards.statement: Navigation TTFB starts after service worker startup completes.
cards.explanation: Navigation TTFB includes service worker startup when a worker participates in the navigation, so initialization contributes to the measured wait.
cards.misconception: Service worker initialization occurs outside navigation TTFB.

cards.statement: Navigation TTFB includes time spent resolving the server hostname.
cards.explanation: DNS lookup falls within navigation TTFB, so network setup contributes alongside waiting for the server response.

cards.statement: Painting a plain CSS background color can trigger FCP.
cards.explanation: A plain background-color paint can mark First Paint, but FCP waits for content such as text or an image.
cards.misconception: Any nonblank paint qualifies as contentful.

cards.statement: Waiting for a web font can delay FCP on a text-first page.
cards.explanation: When font loading holds back the first visible text, that wait contributes to the time before FCP.

cards.statement: The Chrome UX Report includes browsing experiences collected from Microsoft Edge.
cards.explanation: CrUX collects eligible Chrome experiences; sharing the Chromium engine does not make Edge data eligible.
cards.misconception: CrUX aggregates data from any Chromium-based browser.
cards.appliesTo: Chrome UX Report collection policy, checked 2026-10-03
cards.volatilityNote: CrUX browser and platform eligibility can change.

cards.statement: An eligible CrUX origin includes experiences on pages that lack page-level CrUX data.
cards.explanation: Origin aggregation includes eligible user experiences across its pages, even when individual pages fail page-level eligibility.

cards.statement: The CrUX API groups its current field performance measurements into calendar-month reporting periods.
cards.explanation: The CrUX API reports a rolling 28-day collection period, rather than a fixed calendar-month period.
cards.misconception: The API uses fixed monthly reporting periods.

cards.statement: PageSpeed Insights displays available origin field data when page-level data is insufficient.
cards.explanation: PageSpeed Insights falls back to available origin data when a URL lacks enough CrUX samples for page-level reporting.

cards.statement: PageSpeed Insights accepts good LCP and CLS for a pass when INP data is insufficient.
cards.explanation: With insufficient INP data, PageSpeed Insights bases its pass assessment on good LCP and CLS at the 75th percentile.

cards.statement: A typical lab page-load test starts with a returning visitor's populated browser cache.
cards.explanation: Lab tests typically start with a cold cache, whereas returning visitors in field data may reuse cached resources.
cards.misconception: A standard lab load simulates a repeat visitor with cached assets.

source.title: Why lab and field data can be different (and what to do about it)

cards.statement: Lighthouse's page-load CLS result includes shifts caused by scrolling through the page.
cards.explanation: A load-only lab run sees shifts during loading, not the later browsing activity captured by field measurements.
cards.misconception: A page-load lab result covers the rest of a real visit.

source.title: Why lab and field data can be different (and what to do about it)

cards.statement: Local INP in Chrome DevTools reflects the interactions performed during the test.
cards.explanation: A DevTools local INP result characterizes the interactions exercised in that test, rather than a population of real visits.

cards.statement: A good TBT result establishes that real users also experience good INP.
cards.explanation: TBT is a useful lab proxy for INP, but a good TBT result does not establish good real-user INP.
cards.misconception: A proxy metric proves the corresponding real-user result.

cards.statement: The web-vitals library builds its metric measurements on browser performance APIs.
cards.explanation: The web-vitals library adds metric-specific logic over browser performance APIs for real-user measurement.

source.title: Getting started with measuring Web Vitals

cards.statement: LargestContentfulPaint has Baseline support across the major browser engines.
cards.explanation: MDN marks LargestContentfulPaint as Baseline 2025, newly available across current browsers since December 2025.
cards.volatilityNote: Baseline maturity and browser compatibility can change; older browsers may lack this API.

cards.statement: LayoutShift has Baseline support across the major browser engines.
cards.explanation: MDN marks LayoutShift as experimental and not Baseline because support remains limited.
cards.misconception: LayoutShift has the same cross-engine availability as established performance APIs.
cards.volatilityNote: LayoutShift implementation and Baseline status can change.

cards.statement: An inline SVG made of vector paths can qualify as an LCP image candidate.
cards.explanation: LCP considers an image element inside SVG, rather than treating a vector-only SVG drawing as an image candidate.
cards.misconception: Inline SVG vector drawings qualify like embedded raster images.

cards.statement: LCP considers CSS url() background images as possible candidates for the largest element.
cards.explanation: LCP image candidates include elements whose CSS backgrounds load images through url().

cards.statement: A video's first displayed frame supplies its LCP timing when it arrives before the poster.
cards.explanation: For video, LCP uses the earlier of the poster image load time and the first frame presentation time.

cards.statement: A large visible heading is eligible to become a page's LCP element.
cards.explanation: LCP considers block-level elements containing text, so a large heading or paragraph can be the candidate.

cards.statement: Chromium treats a background image covering the entire viewport as an eligible LCP candidate.
cards.explanation: Chromium excludes full-viewport elements as a heuristic for filtering backgrounds rather than main content.
cards.misconception: The largest possible visible background automatically qualifies.
cards.volatilityNote: Browser LCP candidate-filtering heuristics can change.

cards.statement: Upscaling lets an LCP image's reported area exceed its intrinsic image area.
cards.explanation: LCP compensates for image upscaling, so CSS enlargement does not let the reported area exceed the image's intrinsic area.
cards.misconception: CSS enlargement increases measured image size beyond its intrinsic dimensions.

cards.statement: LCP includes a text block's CSS padding when calculating its candidate area.
cards.explanation: LCP sizes text using the bounds of its text nodes, excluding CSS padding, borders, and margins.
cards.misconception: LCP measures the decorated CSS box rather than the text area.

cards.statement: Rendering a larger eligible candidate causes the LCP API to emit a new entry.
cards.explanation: The LCP API reports successive record-size candidates as they render, rather than reporting just one initial candidate.

cards.statement: Removing the LCP candidate from the DOM leaves its earlier qualifying paint in the record.
cards.explanation: Removing an element does not undo its earlier qualifying paint or erase its candidacy from LCP reporting.

cards.statement: The LCP API continues selecting new candidates after the user starts scrolling.
cards.explanation: LCP candidate reporting stops at user input such as scrolling; later renders do not extend that load measurement.
cards.misconception: LCP keeps following content as the user scrolls.

cards.statement: Google's LCP tools exclude visits whose page load starts in a background tab.
cards.explanation: Background-tab loads are excluded from LCP because timing them would not represent a visible loading experience.

cards.statement: A parent page's LargestContentfulPaint entries include candidates rendered inside its iframes.
cards.explanation: The LCP metric includes iframe content, but the parent page's API entries do not expose those iframe candidates.
cards.misconception: Top-level API entries cover descendant browsing contexts.

cards.statement: The LCP sub-part timeline starts when the browser receives the first HTML byte.
cards.explanation: The LCP breakdown includes TTFB, beginning when navigation starts rather than when the HTML response arrives.
cards.misconception: Time before the HTML response sits outside the LCP breakdown.

cards.statement: web.dev measures LCP resource load delay from TTFB until the LCP resource request starts.
cards.explanation: Resource load delay captures the gap before the browser begins fetching the LCP resource.

cards.statement: LCP resource load duration includes waiting to display an image after its download finishes.
cards.explanation: Waiting after the LCP resource finishes loading belongs to element render delay, not resource load duration.
cards.misconception: The resource loading phase continues until the browser paints the image.

cards.statement: A text LCP element using a system font has zero resource load delay and duration.
cards.explanation: System-font text needs no LCP resource download, so both resource-loading sub-parts are zero.

cards.statement: web.dev suggests allocating roughly 40% of the overall LCP time to resource load duration.
cards.explanation: The suggested breakdown allocates about 40% to resource loading; it is an optimization target, not a required ratio.

cards.statement: The preload scanner discovers an LCP image URL stored inside an external JavaScript bundle.
cards.explanation: The preload scanner scans HTML, not JavaScript source. An image URL in the initial HTML is discoverable before application code runs.
cards.misconception: The preload scanner extracts asset URLs from application JavaScript.

cards.statement: web.dev recommends lazy-loading the LCP image to reduce loading contention.
cards.explanation: web.dev explicitly advises against lazy-loading the LCP image because it delays discovery and loading of critical content.
cards.misconception: General lazy-loading advice also applies to the LCP image.

cards.statement: In Chrome, fetchpriority="high" gives an LCP image high priority from its initial request.
cards.explanation: Chrome starts an image marked fetchpriority="high" at high priority instead of waiting for layout to promote it.
cards.volatilityNote: Chrome can change its resource-priority implementation.

source.title: Optimize resource loading with the Fetch Priority API

cards.statement: Preloading a CSS background LCP image lets its request start before the stylesheet reveals its URL.
cards.explanation: An HTML preload exposes a CSS background image early, bypassing the stylesheet-discovery dependency.

source.title: Preload critical assets to improve loading speed

cards.statement: The browser paints a downloaded LCP image while an initial, matching head stylesheet is still loading.
cards.explanation: A completed image download does not bypass render-blocking CSS; the browser waits for the required stylesheet before painting.
cards.misconception: Finishing the image download overrides stylesheet rendering dependencies.

cards.statement: A fully client-rendered page exposes its LCP content when application JavaScript finishes downloading.
cards.explanation: Client-rendered content still needs JavaScript execution to build the DOM; completing the script download is not enough.
cards.misconception: Downloading application code is sufficient to expose client-rendered content.

cards.statement: Serving HTML from a nearby cache can reduce the TTFB portion of LCP.
cards.explanation: A nearby cache can avoid a distant origin round trip and repeated HTML generation, shortening the wait for the response.
